signals.title: @elenaantoniou3: The core of the broken pledge lies in a promise made during Google's 2014 acquisition of DeepMind, and a series of events that dismantled it
signals.content: The core of the broken pledge lies in a promise made during Google's 2014 acquisition of DeepMind, and a series of events that dismantled it step-by-step. 📜 The 2014 Promise When Google acquired DeepMind for around $400-500 million, it was conditional on an unprecedented, legally binding agreement: an independent ethics board to ensure the AI would never be misused for military purposes. This "Do No Harm" principle was a core condition of the deal. ⚔️ The Two "Drops" The pledge didn't break overnight; it was chipped away in two major moves: · The First Crack (2018: Project Maven): Google allowed its AI to analyze military drone footage. 4,000 employees signed a petition, and Google backed out, formally pledging not to develop AI for weapons or surveillance. · The Point of No Return (2025-2026): Leadership quietly removed the weapons/surveillance ban from the official AI principles. They then signed a classified deal allowing the Pentagon to use Gemini for "any lawful purpose" on secret networks. 💔 The Betrayal and Unionization Staff saw this as a direct betrayal of the 2014 promise. Fearing their AI could enable "lethal autonomous weapons and mass surveillance," over 600 employees signed an open letter and launched a unionization drive to force an ethics oversight body. So, the original promise did exist, but the same company that made it eventually prioritized government contracts over the founding principle. The classified nature of the Pentagon deal is a huge part of why employees are so powerless—want me to explain why the "black box" secrecy makes their fears worse?

signals.title: Long-Horizon AI Research for Grothendieck Constant: A Case Study in Human-AI Mathematical Collaboration
signals.content: AI agents are increasingly used in mathematics research, but it is often unclear how to use them effectively. Towards this, we present an extensive case study of how AI was used to improve bounds on the Grothendieck constant $K_G$, which captures the hardness between combinatorial problems and their continuous relaxations. Specifically, while the precise value of $K_G$ is not known, we recently tightened the best known bounds to \[ \frac{6π}{11} \;\le\; K_G \;\le\; \fracπ{2\log(1+\sqrt2)} - 10^{-4}. \] Crucially, these improvements were achieved using an AI research system that could arrive at insights deemed novel by domain experts. We give a detailed discussion of our experience using AI for mathematics research, particularly touching upon its strengths and weaknesses, as well as our experience with creating ideal conditions for AI to arrive at breakthrough insights.

signals.title: Generative AI use in Statistical Research: A Literature Review and Code Generation Case Study
signals.content: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is a large language model (LLM) that has the ability to generate media based on user-provided prompts. Given the demonstrated capabilities of models such as ChatGPT in information synthesis and programming, there is growing interest in their potential role within the research process. However, little work has evaluated recent GenAI models for research tasks in the domain of statistical research. This case study examines GenAI as a tool for developing a literature review and translating methodology from academic papers into code, for the topic of dynamic treatment regime (DTR) estimation via the dynamic weighted ordinary least squares (dWOLS) approach. Specifically, we utilize ChatGPT-5 and ScholarAI (Sept-Nov 2025 release) in the processes of identifying relevant sources for the literature review, creating summaries of papers, identifying gaps in research, and R code generation to implement methodology. Our findings show that current GenAI models lack the depth and contextual understanding required to accomplish these tasks without careful prompting and supervision of a knowledgeable researcher. Nonetheless, GenAI has potential to increase efficiency of tasks which take advantage of its search and summarization abilities, as well as basic code debugging and algorithm formation. We demonstrate that under a knowledgeable guide, GenAI can function as a research tool, but not as a substitute for methodological expertise.
